Network Intrusion Prevention: Deploy layered inline controls that prevent automated access based on observed request and session behavior rather than relying solely on challenge presentation. Use silent challenges, browser/client validation, rate controls, and bot-management signals to pre

name: Steal Application Specific Passwords
desc: Adversaries may steal Application Specific Passwords (ASPs) to gain access to Valid Accounts, bypassing multifactor authentication (MFA) methods. ASPs are passwords typically used to give third-party applications or legacy devices (which do not support MFA methods) account access. An adversary may socially engineer a user into providing an ASP (using methods like Phishing for Information), generate an ASP for an already compromised account, or obtain an ASP stored on a system. Afterward, adversaries may use the ASP to access Valid Accounts and, in some cases, maintain Persistence, bypassing any form of MFA set on the account.
mitigations: User Training: ASPs can be obtained through social engineering, which your technique explicitly includes. Train users not to generate or disclose ASPs in response to unsolicited instructions.

Disable or Remove Feature or Program: Disable ASP functionality where modern authentication is available. Microsoft specifically supports disabling users' ability to create app passwords and recommends disabling legacy authentication so existing app passwords no longer work.

Account Use Policies: Restrict authentication paths/clients/locations through which accounts using legacy/app-password authentication can authenticate. This matters because an ASP that has been stolen shouldn't automatically have unrestricted account reach.

User Account Management: Restrict which users may create/use ASPs; disable ASP creation where unnecessary; remove existing ASPs. Microsoft allows admins to disable creation and separately delete existing ASPs; Google administrators can view/revoke users' application-specific passwords
examples: APT42 has stolen application specific passwords in order to bypass MFA requirements to include victim environments who leverage the Microsoft App Password feature.

name: Indirect Prompt Injection
desc: Adversaries may deliver malicious prompts to an LLM indirectly by embedding the prompts in content that the adversary expects may be processed by an LLM. These prompts can be included in web pages, documents, emails, tickets, code, or other sources that an agent, copilot, or other AI system may retrieve and process. When an LLM processes this content, the embedded instructions may cause the system to perform unintended behaviors. Adversaries may use indirect prompt injection to Impair Autonomous Defenses, and for unauthorized execution of any capabilities available to the LLM.
mitigations: Restrict File and Directory Permissions: Restrict AI agents to files, directories, repositories, and content stores required for their approved workflows. Limit write access separately from read access where possible to reduce the actions available following successful indirect prompt injection.

Privileged Account Management: Prevent AI agents processing untrusted or externally controlled content from automatically exercising privileged permissions. Require additional authorization for sensitive operations derived from retrieved content.

Execution Prevention: Prevent instructions contained in retrieved or externally supplied content from independently authorizing consequential agent actions. Require tool/API requests derived from external content to satisfy authorization and policy controls independent of the model

Network Segmentation: Restrict network resources and external destinations accessible to AI agents that process untrusted content. Limit outbound communication and access to unrelated internal services to reduce exfiltration and lateral effects following successful injection.

User Account Management: Use dedicated identities for AI agents and restrict their permissions to the minimum resources and actions required by the approved workflow. Do not allow retrieved content to change the authorization context associated with the agent.

name: Direct Prompt Injection
desc: Adversaries may input malicious prompts directly into an LLM’s user interface. The prompts can be designed to bypass safeguards, manipulate context, override previous instructions, or coerce the LLM into unauthorized behavior. Adversaries may use direct prompt injection to Generate Content prohibited by the LLM's guardrails or to induce the system to utilize its capabilities in unintended or prohibited ways. Adversaries may achieve this by instructing the LLM to ignore previous instructions or safety rules, or by impersonating a role such as a researcher or privileged user.
mitigations: User Account Management: Associate AI interactions with authenticated identities and constrain AI-mediated actions to the permissions of the initiating user. Do not allow prompt content to establish or elevate the authorization context used by downstream tools or services.

Execution Prevention: Prevent user-supplied AI prompts from directly authorizing consequential actions. Enforce tool, API, command, and resource authorization outside the model and reject requested actions that exceed the permissions associated with the initiating user or agent tas

User Training: Train users responsible for AI-enabled systems to recognize attempts to manipulate system instructions, role boundaries, or safety controls through user-provided prompts and to independently validate consequential AI-generated actions.

Privileged Account Management: Restrict access to privileged AI capabilities and require explicit authorization or human approval for AI-generated actions involving administrative functions, sensitive resources, or privileged tools.
examples: During the Anthropic AI-orchestrated Campaign, the adversary entered a prompt that claimed the user was an employee of a cybersecurity firm and that Claude was being used for defensive cybersecurity testing to authorize restricted operations.

During the AI-Assisted Breach of Mexico's Government Infrastructure, the adversary abused Claude Code by utilizing a file-write operation within the prompt that created a `claude.md` file that contained a pre-written 1,084-line document containing penetration

name: AI-Enabled Exfiltration
desc: Adversaries may utilize Direct Prompt Injection, Indirect Prompt Injection or other methods to instruct enterprise AI agents to exfiltrate data. When enterprise systems incorporate the use of AI assistants or other AI agents, adversaries may abuse these systems to weaponize sanctioned tools available to the agent. As an AI agent processes queries or ingests data, an injected prompt can cause the agent to use its tool connections in unauthorized or unintended ways. When AI agents are induced to exfiltrate data, other exfiltration techniques likely apply as well to transfer the information out of the network, such as Exfiltration to Code Repository or Exfiltration Over Web Service.
mitigations: User Training: Employ user training to include the implications of AI agent use within corporate environments

Application Isolation and Sandboxing: Ensuring that LLM/AI systems are contained to only within the organizational network with no outside access can contain the exfiltration of sensitive data to within an organizational network.
Restrict File and Directory Permissions: Restrict file permissions to limit the exposure of sensitive data from AI agents.
